children: WINNIPEG, Manitoba--By the time Statistics Canada released its latest satellite imagery-based principal field crop estimates on Sept. 16, the trade was already looking ahead.

StatCan projected the 2026-27 canola crop at 22.1 million tonnes, a 0.8 percent decline from last year's crop. Yields are expected to drop 8.3 percent at 41.2 bushels per acre but harvested area was set to grow to a record 23 million acres. The survey-based principal field crop report from StatCan will be released in December and could see revisions made.
Tony Tryhuk from RBC Dominion Securities in Winnipeg said the whole report didn't have any surprises and the trade already anticipated as such.

"I don't think the market reacted to the report. We're much more focused on any type of harvest delays or potential late-season yield changes," Tryhuk said. "We're also looking forward to demand and what that looks like for the current crop year and look at what the potential ending stock number will be for July 2027."

While he was content with StatCan's production estimate, he said AAFC's August estimate for 2026-27 canola carryout at 1.5 million tonnes was "undersized" and would make up for any potential production loss between now and StatCan's December report.

"I like the (production) number and even if the number tends to trend a little lower due to reduced yields, I still think we're working with a robust total supply number and I think we'll meet our demand expectations ... and still have a comfortable carryout," Tryhuk said, citing open interest, domestic crush and overseas demand from China and Europe.
Canola prices saw earlier gains erased before ending the Sept. 16 session lower. During the week, November canola lost C$5.20 per tonne at $826.90 per tonne.

He said producers should be fortunate to see canola prices exceed C$820 per tonne at a time when harvest pressure typically rears its head. However, Tryhuk thinks that time is coming sooner than later.

"I'm concerned about prices being sustained at these levels," he said. "I know there are still geopolitical risks that our market faces and those should continue to underpin the market ... but what I don't like is rallying during harvest. Historically, that relationship doesn't hold and I should expect prices to move lower and more likely than not, we'll test C$800 before we test C$900."
